title: PRIME – Primary Mediastinal Real-World Evidence: A multicenter retrospective cohort study of mediastinal lymphomas at diagnosis and relapse, with a focus on relapsed/refractory primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL)
summary: Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL) is a rare form of lymph node cancer that mainly affects young adults. Most patients can be cured with their first treatment. In about 10–20%, however, the first therapy is not sufficiently effective or the disease returns. For this situation it is unclear which treatment is best, because the disease is too rare to conduct large comparative trials. In this study, existing treatment data from several hospitals in Germany and Europe are pooled and analysed. We investigate how mediastinal lymphomas are treated, how often relapses occur, which treatments are used at relapse and how successful they are. No study treatment takes place; only data from past treatments are analysed, pooled in pseudonymised form (without names). The results are intended to help improve the treatment of future patients.

interventions.name: Observation group (single arm, non-interventional): patients with histologically confirmed mediastinal lymphoma – PMBCL (primary focus), mediastinal grey zone lymphoma (MGZL), DLBCL or follicular lymphoma with primary mediastinal manifestation, and optionally Hodgkin lymphoma with mediastinal manife

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
(1) Histologically confirmed mediastinal lymphoma: PMBCL, mediastinal grey zone lymphoma (MGZL), DLBCL with primary mediastinal manifestation, follicular lymphoma with primary mediastinal manifestation; optionally Hodgkin lymphoma with mediastinal manifestation as a comparison cohort. (2) First diagnosis and treatment in the anti-CD20 ('rituximab') era (only routine data documented between 1 January 2005 and 10 October 2026 are analysed). (3) Treatment or co-treatment at a participating centre. (4) First-diagnosis and/or relapse setting. Pregnancy at the time of diagnosis/therapy is not an exclusion criterion.
Exclusion criteria:
(1) Lack of histological confirmation. (2) Lack of clinical documentation of the core variables (diagnosis, first-line therapy, course, vital status).
